statement: In calculus, the chain rule is a formula expressing the derivative of the composition of differentiable functions in terms of their individual derivatives. In Leibniz notation, for $y = f(u)$ and $u = g(x)$, it is given by $\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{dy}{du} \cdot \frac{du}{dx}$, and for a three-function composition $y = f(u), u = g(v), v = h(x)$ at $x = a$, by $\left.\frac{dy}{dx}\right|_{x=a} = \left.\frac{dy}{du}\right|_{u=g(h(a))} \cdot \left.\frac{du}{dv}\right|_{v=h(a)} \cdot \left.\frac{dv}{dx}\right|_{x=a}$, or in Lagrange notation as $(f \circ g \circ h)'(a) = f'((g \circ h)(a)) \cdot g'(h(a)) \cdot h'(a)$. The supplied source text does not contain a derivation of the chain rule itself (the proof section truncates after the opening sentence), so this concept is stated as a definition.

symbols.meaning: intermediate variable in a three-function composite
arbitrary composition of n functions f_1 o ... o f_n

properties.property: Associativity / composition of three functions: (f o g o h)'(a) = f'((g o h)(a)) * g'(h(a)) * h'(a) = (f o g)'(h(a)) * h'(a)
properties.why: Follows from decomposing the composite function as either f o (g o h) or (f o g) o h and applying the chain rule

properties.property: Arbitrary n-fold composition: f_{1..n}'(x) = prod_{k=1}^n f_k'(f_{(k+1..n)}(x)) and D f_{1..n} = prod_{k=1}^n [D f_k o f_{(k+1..n)}]
properties.why: Follows by repeated application of the chain rule to an n-fold function composition
Follows by expressing f(x)/g(x) as f(x) * (1/g(x)) and combining the product rule with the chain rule applied to the reciprocal function

properties.property: Inverse function derivative formula: f'(y) = 1 / g'(f(y)) where x = f(y) is the inverse of y = g(x)
properties.why: Follows by differentiating the identity f(g(x)) = x using the chain rule to obtain f'(g(x))g'(x) = 1 and substituting x = f(y)

properties.property: Higher derivatives via Faà di Bruno's formula: e.g., d^2y/dx^2 = (d^2y/du^2)(du/dx)^2 + (dy/du)(d^2u/dx^2)
properties.why: Follows from generalizing the chain rule to higher-order derivatives through successive differentiation

properties.property: Algorithmic foundation of backpropagation in deep learning
properties.why: Forms the basis of gradient descent optimization in neural networks by propagating derivatives through composite layers

assumptions.assumption: The constituent functions are differentiable at the corresponding points of composition
assumptions.breaks_when: Any component function is non-differentiable at its evaluation point

assumptions.assumption: In inverse function differentiation, g is differentiable and its inverse f is differentiable with g'(f(y)) != 0
assumptions.breaks_when: g'(f(y)) = 0, causing division by zero, or the inverse function f is not differentiable at that point (e.g., g(x) = x^3 at x = 0)

failure_modes.mode: Division by zero in inverse function derivative
failure_modes.cause: The derivative g'(f(y)) equals zero, occurring when the inverse function f is not differentiable at y (e.g., g(x) = x^3 and f(y) = y^(1/3) at y = 0)

failure_modes.signature: Derivative does not exist or difference quotient fails to converge
failure_modes.cause: One of the component functions in the composition is not differentiable at the evaluated intermediate point
